newsitem.title: MEXICO: Feel-good factor seeps into Mexican economy.
newsitem.headline: Feel-good factor seeps into Mexican economy.

text.p: The much-trumpeted recovery in the Mexican economy is at last leaving the abstract realm of statistics and spreading into the domain of corner shops and the bigger department stores, economists say.

As Mexico emerges from a mid-year corporate results season that has left more analysts pleased than disappointed, economists say the feel-good factor is starting to reach parts of the economy previously excluded from the recovery.
"From a very unbalanced growth (story), the recovery has become much more balanced in (the last) six months," said Damian Fraser, director at Caspian Securities here.
While the Mexican economy grew 5.1 percent in 1996, that growth was primarily industry and export-led.
Its benefits were felt so little in the pockets of ordinary Mexicans that many took revenge on the ruling party in mid-term elections in July.
But now the recovery is starting to fan out into sectors of the economy other than industry and exports.

"We're seeing a more rounded recovery than we had last year -- this year you'll probably get the same (economic) growth, or maybe even less, but you'll feel it much more strongly because it's more balanced," Fraser said.

Recent corporate results bear out impressions the recovery is starting to broaden. The consumer sector has started to back up official data showing a first half rise in department store sales of 4.8 percent and an increase in retail sales.
Retail sales climbed 6.6 percent in April and 4.4 percent in May -- the first two months to show any improvement since the 1994 peso crash plunged Mexico into recession.
Rogelio Ramirez de la O, director of economic advisers Ecanal, said lower debt levels, declining inflation and the persistently strong peso were helping sales.
"Because of the lower debt pressure you are seeing people buy durable goods -- you're seeing that in stores like Liverpool and Sears," he said.
Beverage firms like Femsa and Modelo this quarter performed much better than forecast, while retailers Comercial Mexicana and Liverpool both showed higher same-store sales than foreseen.
Analysts also pointed to the success of media companies like Televisa, whose healthy results signal a rise in advertising geared to the returning consumer.

Although purchasing power remains unspectacular, analysts say an increase in registered employment translates into more shoppers scurrying through shopping malls, at least in Mexico City and the wealthier north.
A breakdown of same-store sales bears this out, with retailers seeing more shoppers than they did last year, even if those shoppers are not yet walking out with baskets piled high.
More than 1.5 million Mexicans lost their jobs as a direct result of the 1994-95 recession. But official statistics suggest this too is on the mend.
"The trend is clear towards lower unemployment," said Marilyn Skiles, managing director for Latin American research at Chase Manhattan Bank.

"There has also been a pick-up in real wages, although it is still very small," she added, pointing to manufacturing sector salaries that in April registered their first rise since 1994, albeit just 0.4 percent.
UBS this week raised its weighting for Mexico in a Latin American portfolio, pinned squarely on a rebound in consumption.
But analysts agree Mexico also needs a resumption in credit growth, and said there were nascent signs of this in some of the banking results.
Fraser said he expected the trend to turn even further towards the domestic economy for the rest of the year, particularly if the peso keeps up its stubborn strength.
"If the peso stays where it is, we expect export growth to slow and the recovery to be more domestic-based in the next six-month period," he said.
